facts.fact: Name for the term: "Vây hậu môn"
Name for the term: "anal fin"
The anal fin is a median fin on the underside of the fish. Standen and Lauder hypothesize that it produces a sideways force below the centre of mass, offsetting the dorsal fin's force.
In studies of perch, sunfish and trout, the dorsal and anal fins worked together as force producers and stabilizers during swimming.
In male livebearers (Poeciliidae), the gonopodium develops from anal fin rays 3–5, the so-called 3–4–5 complex, during sexual maturation.
Gonopodium development is triggered by rising sex steroids. Elevated testosterone makes a subset of anal fin rays change shape, and adding testosterone can make juveniles grow one.
In male guppies (cá bảy màu, Poecilia reticulata), the anal fin develops into a sexual organ called the gonopodium.
In male guppies (Poecilia reticulata), the gonopodium is an anal fin changed into a tube that is hard and long. It sits behind the pelvic fins, near the vent.
Female guppies (Poecilia reticulata) keep a normal anal fin that is triangular and soft.
Male livebearers have a rod-shaped anal fin used for internal fertilisation. Females have a standard fan-shaped anal fin.
The anal-fin difference shows from about 4 to 6 weeks of age in guppies, and slightly later in larger livebearers.

At 2–3 weeks old, a male guppy's (Poecilia reticulata) anal fin starts turning into a gonopodium but is still short and soft. The gonopodium is clearer at 1–2 months and fully developed at 3–4 months.
To see a guppy's (Poecilia reticulata) sexual organ, use a magnifying glass or keep the fish in good light.
Female livebearers carrying fry show a dark gravid spot near the anal fin.
Males of Goodeidae and Hemirhamphidae (halfbeaks) have modified, flexible anal fin rays called an andropodium, which make the fin look notched.
The andropodium of Goodeidae is used to clasp the female during mating, not for insemination like the gonopodium in Poeciliidae.
Juvenile fish are often impossible to sex reliably. Wait until a species reaches at least 60 to 70% of adult size.
Swordtail males that develop late may grow their sword at six months or older.
Some breeders cut short the gonopodium of long-finned male guppies (Poecilia reticulata) so they can fertilise females.
Ragged fins can affect all fin types, particularly the caudal, dorsal and anal fins.
Ragged fins can be caused by tankmates nipping, including at night when it may go unnoticed.
Sharp-edged decor, including some plastic plants and rough rocks, can catch and tear fins.
Poor water quality can let bacteria infect damaged fins, turning ragged fins into fin rot.
For ragged fins, first test the water and do a 25–50% water change with conditioned, temperature-matched water.
Ragged fins with clean edges and no infection need no medication. For mild antiseptic support, the page suggests aquarium salt at one tablespoon per five gallons while the fins heal.
To prevent fin damage, remove sharp decor, cover filter intakes, and separate or remove aggressive tankmates. A hospital tank can help.
